verifyText.value: What Type of Financing Is Best for My Business?

waitForText.value: What Type of Financing Is Best for My Business?

verifyText.value: When you own a small business, finding the right kind of financing can be key to weathering those periods when cash is in short supply due to sales seasonality, accounts receivable lagging behind, unexpected expenses, emergencies, or other reasons. Common solutions for working capital needs include business credit cards, overdraft protection, business lines of credit, and business term loans. Knowing the pros and cons of each option will help you decide which is best for your business.

A business credit card is intended for use by a business rather than for an individual's personal use. It offers convenience, ease of qualification, and simplified bookkeeping. It provides an easy way to build up a positive business credit history and some offer rewards such as airline miles or cash back. However, this revolving line of credit is usually for a smaller amount and higher interest rate than what you would get with a traditional line of credit or term loan. A business credit card must also be carefully managed. If payments are not made on time or in full, the interest rate can escalate quickly and your personal credit rating may be harmed.

A line of credit linked to a business checking account, business overdraft protection supports your business through unexpected cash flow shortages. This allows your business to avoid overdraft penalties and continue to run without worrying that outstanding checks or automated payments will not clear.

A business line of credit is a revolving business loan ideal for businesses that go through seasonal fluctuations in sales (while expenses remain the same) and/or need short-term access to funds for a variety of business needs. It operates similar to a credit card in that you use it as you need it, can borrow or use more as your principal is paid down, and your payments only reflect the amount of money you've borrowed. If your balance is zero, you won't have a payment. The interest rate on a line of credit is typically lower than on a credit card or term loan and closing costs are generally minimal. Lines of credit can be unsecured or secured. However, if you're late on a payment or exceed your credit line, your interest rates may increase substantially.

With a business term loan, you borrow a lump sum of money, get it all at once and pay it back over a fixed time period. Your monthly payment begins immediately and doesn't change from month to month, whether you're using all the money or not. Closing costs and interest rates for term loans are typically higher than those on a business line of credit or credit card. And, unlike a revolving line of credit, once you pay off the loan, you'll have to reapply for a new loan if you need more funds. In addition, term loans are typically used for a specific purpose and secured by collateral but there are unsecured options.
Before offering financing over a certain limit to small businesses, lenders typically analyze the creditworthiness of the borrower by using the Five C's:

is your ability to repay the loan and is generally the most important of the five factors. Lenders will consider your revenues and expenses, the timing of your cash flows, outstanding debt, your credit history, and other possible sources of repayment.
refers to something that you own to cover loan repayment in case of default. Examples include real estate (personal or commercial), accounts receivable, inventory, and equipment.

represents the amount of money you have personally invested in the business which could be lost if the business fails. Before committing to any funding, lenders will expect owner investment to be significant.

are two-fold. First, condition refers to external factors that will impact the future success of your business e.g. overall economic climate, the health of your industry, the degree of competition, etc. Second, conditions refer to the purpose of the loan. Will the money be used for working capital, additional equipment, inventory, or expansion?

is a highly subjective assessment of the business owner's trustworthiness with regard to repaying the loan and generating a return on the investment. Your educational background, business experience, and references, and reputation will be examined.

This tool is provided for the education and illustrative purposes only. The accuracy of the calculations and their applicability to your circumstances are not guaranteed. Please consult your financial, tax or legal advisor regarding your unique situation.
